tasks.task_description: Task 1: For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, South America), select the country most critical in terms of HIV/AIDS. Build a model to approximate the expected rate of change in the number of HIV/AIDS infections for these countries from 2006 to 2050, in the absence of any additional interventions. Explain the model, its assumptions, and how the countries were selected.
tasks.task_analysis: Country selection: From the WHO member states list, I selected the country with the highest 1999 HIV burden (from the 'global hiv-aids cases, 1999' sheet) in each continental region. Africa: South Africa (4.2M HIV+, highest in sub-Saharan Africa by a wide margin). Asia: India (3.7M, largest absolute burden in Asia). Europe: Romania (7,000, highest in Eastern Europe among WHO members with reported data). North America: Brazil (540,000, highest in Latin America/Caribbean). Australia: Australia (14,000, the only country in the Oceania region with a meaningful HIV burden among WHO members). The second African country, Uganda (820,000), was also modeled because its epidemic trajectory differs qualitatively from South Africa's (still growing vs. peaked). Concentrated vs. generalized: South Africa, Uganda, and Brazil have generalized epidemics (peaked 2003-2005, now on the plateau/early-decline part of the S-curve). India, China, Romania, and Australia have concentrated epidemics (still rising, growth decaying to zero by 2025-2030). This distinction is critical: the same intervention will have very different marginal effects depending on where the epidemic is in its lifecycle.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State variable: I(t) = number living with HIV, ages 0-49, in country c at year t. Baseline (no interventions): I_base(t) follows a country-specific epidemic curve anchored to I(2006). For generalized epidemics: I_base(t) = I_2006 * (1 + r)^(t-2006) for t < t_peak, then flat, where r is a small annual growth/decline rate (South Africa r=+0.8%/yr through 2010 then 0; Uganda r=0; Brazil r=-0.5%/yr). For concentrated epidemics: I_base(t) = I_2006 * prod_{y=2006}^{t-1} (1 + g_y), where g_y = g_0 * max(0, 1 - (y-2006)/(t_peak-2006)) is a linearly decaying growth rate (g_0 = 3-5%/yr) that reaches zero at t_peak, then -0.2%/yr thereafter. This produces the S-curve shape: rapid early growth, peak 10-20+ years after introduction, then slow decline. The baseline is self-consistent: it reflects the combined effect of new infections, HIV mortality, and aging out of the 0-49 window. Annual rate of change: dI/dt = I(t) - I(t-1). For 2006-2016: South Africa +14,364/yr, Uganda -991/yr, India +112,426/yr, China +11,728/yr, Romania +288/yr, Brazil -1,106/yr, Australia +119/yr. For 2045-2055: South Africa 0/yr, Uganda -1,534/yr, India -11,399/yr, China -1,382/yr, Romania -24/yr, Brazil 0/yr, Australia -31/yr. Parameter table: r (annual baseline growth rate, generalized): South Africa [0, 0.01], Uganda [0, 0], Brazil [-0.01, 0]; source: calibrated to UNAIDS 2003-2010 prevalence trajectories. g_0 (initial growth rate, concentrated): India [0.02, 0.04], China [0.015, 0.035], Romania [0.03, 0.05], Australia [0.005, 0.015]; source: exchange 10 (rapid early growth, peak 10-20+ years after introduction). t_peak: India 2028, China 2024, Romania 2020, Australia 2030; source: exchange 10.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The baseline model shows that without interventions, the total number of people living with HIV in the six selected countries will remain roughly stable through 2050, with concentrated epidemics (India, China) peaking in the 2020s and then slowly declining, while generalized epidemics (South Africa, Uganda, Brazil) are already on the plateau or in slow decline. The rate of change is dominated by new infections offset by HIV mortality and aging out of the 0-49 window. Limitations: (1) The baseline curves are stylized S-curves, not mechanistic compartmental models; they capture the aggregate trajectory but not the age-structure dynamics. (2) The 1999 data is a snapshot; I(2006) is estimated by extrapolating from 1999 using the epidemic phase, which introduces uncertainty. (3) The model does not capture behavioral changes (condom use, needle exchange, etc.) that are already happening in 2006 and will continue; it is a 'no additional interventions' baseline, not a 'no interventions at all' counterfactual. (4) The 0-49 age window is an artifact of the 1999 dataset; the true burden includes 50+ year olds, who are a growing share as the epidemic ages.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Estimate the level of financial resources from foreign aid donors realistically expected to be available to address HIV/AIDS, by year, from 2006 to 2050, for the selected countries. Use the Task 1 model and these resource estimates to estimate the expected rate of change in HIV/AIDS infections under three scenarios: (1) ARV drug therapy, (2) a preventative HIV/AIDS vaccine, (3) both. Assume no drug-resistant strains (Task 3 addresses this).
tasks.task_analysis: Financial resources: Global AIDS foreign aid was approximately $4.5 billion in 2006, rising at ~$1.25 billion per year to ~$10 billion by 2009-2011 (PEPFAR $15B/5yr, Global Fund ramp, World Bank MAP, bilateral donors), then flattening due to donor fatigue, with a modest 1%/yr growth from 2030 onward. This is a rapid but bounded ramp, not an open-ended commitment. The six low/middle-income countries (South Africa, Uganda, India, China, Brazil, Romania) receive 85% of their share (the other 15% covers prevention, testing, etc.); the share is allocated by 1999 HIV burden. High-income countries (Australia, Romania) self-finance ARV access from their own health budgets (Appendix 1: 53% and 64% of advanced-HIV adults already on ARVs). ARV model: Treatment capacity arvs(t) = min(cov_target(t) * I(t-1), cap_t, fund(t)/1100). cov_target rises from 10% in 2006 to 20% in 2010, 55% in 2020, and 70% by 2030+ (exchange 5: under 10-15% in 2006, 40-60% by mid-2010s, 60-80%+ long run). cap_t = cap0 * 1.25^min(t-2005, 10) represents health-system scaling that plateaus after 10 years. The fraction of infected on ARV is supp(t) = n3(t)/I(t-1), where n3(t) = n3(t-1)*0.70 + arvs(t) (70% adherence, exchange 1: 60-75% reliably adherent). ARV reduces new infections by a factor of (1 - 0.92*supp), where 0.92 is the transmission reduction from viral suppression (exchange 2: treated state suppresses viral load; relapse restores infectiousness). The baseline curve already embeds natural mortality, so ARV's mortality effect is a second-order correction that I neglect for clarity. Vaccine model: Available 2015 (default) or 2010 (Task 4 R&D front-loading). New cohorts (infants) are protected at the DTP3 coverage rate; adults are protected at the TT2 rate via booster campaigns. Protection lasts 4 years (exchange 6: 3-5 years), with boosters every 4 years. Efficacy is 40% (exchange 7: 30-50%). vacc_share(t) = 0.4*DTP3 + 0.6*adult_coverage(t). The vaccine reduces new infections by a factor of (1 - 0.40*vacc_share). Cost is $0.75/dose, negligible compared to ARV.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: ARV scenario: I(t) = I(t-1) * (1 + r_base(t) * (1 - 0.92*supp(t))), where r_base(t) is the baseline annual growth rate and supp(t) = n3(t)/I(t-1). n3(t) = 0.70*n3(t-1) + arvs(t). arvs(t) = min(cov_target(t)*I(t-1), cap_t, fund(t)/1100). cov_target(t) = 0.10 + 0.025*(t-2006) for t<2010; 0.20 + 0.035*(t-2010) for 2010<=t<2020; min(0.70, 0.55 + 0.005*(t-2020)) for t>=2020. cap_t = cap0 * 1.25^min(t-2005, 10). fund(t) = aid_global(t) * burden_share * 0.85 for low/middle-income; full access for high-income. aid_global(t) = 4.5e9 + (t-2005)*1.25e9 for t<2009; 10e9 for 2009<=t<2030; 10e9 * 1.01^(t-2030) for t>=2030. Vaccine scenario: I(t) = I(t-1) * (1 + r_base(t) * (1 - 0.40*vacc_share(t))). vacc_share(t) = 0.4*DTP3 + 0.6*v0(t), where v0(t) starts at 0.30*TT2 in vac_year, increases by 0.25/yr, resets to TT2 every 4 years. Both: I(t) = I(t-1) * (1 + r_base(t) * (1 - 0.92*supp(t)) * (1 - 0.40*vacc_share(t))). Parameter table: ARV cost $1,100/patient/yr, interval [800, 1500], source: task statement (DOTS < $1100). Adherence pA = 0.70, interval [0.60, 0.75], source: exchange 1. Transmission reduction e_ARV = 0.92, interval [0.85, 0.95], source: exchange 2 (viral suppression ~90%+). Treatment coverage target: 10% 2006, 20% 2010, 55% 2020, 70% 2030+, interval [0.10, 0.70], source: exchange 5. Vaccine efficacy 0.40, interval [0.30, 0.50], source: exchange 7. Vaccine duration 4 yr, interval [3, 5], source: exchange 6. Global aid $4.5B 2006, +$1.25B/yr to $10B by 2009, flat to 2030, +1%/yr after, source: exchange 8. DTP3 rates: South Africa 0.82, Uganda 0.72, India 0.70, China 0.98, Romania 0.78, Brazil 0.96, Australia 0.93; TT2 rates: South Africa 0.52, Uganda 0.50, India 0.86, China 0.34, Romania 0.375, Brazil 0.47, Australia 0.34; source: vaccination_rate_data.xls (WHO 2002).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: ARV scenario (2006-2055): South Africa I2050 = 4.57M (vs. 4.58M baseline), dN/dt 2006-16 = +13,181/yr (vs. +14,364), 2.79M on ARV by 2050. Uganda I2050 = 0.79M (vs. 0.77M), dN/dt 2006-16 = -783/yr (vs. -991). India I2050 = 5.07M (vs. 5.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +76,878/yr (vs. +112,426), 4.66M on ARV by 2050. China I2050 = 0.65M (vs. 0.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +7,295/yr (vs. +11,728). Brazil I2050 = 0.55M (vs. 0.55M), dN/dt 2006-16 = -771/yr (vs. -1,106). Australia I2050 = 0.01M (vs. 0.02M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +55/yr (vs. +119). The ARV scenario reduces the rate of new infections by 20-45% in the growing countries (India, China) and slows the decline slightly in the plateauing countries (South Africa, Uganda, Brazil). The effect is most pronounced in India, where the concentrated epidemic is still growing rapidly; ARV reduces the 2006-2016 growth rate from +112,426/yr to +76,878/yr. By 2050, 2.39-4.66M people are on ARV in the six countries, with 0.32-2.28M in the failing/resistant pool (see Task 3). Vaccine scenario (2010 start, 2006-2055): South Africa I2050 = 4.57M (vs. 4.58M baseline), dN/dt 2006-16 = +13,434/yr (vs. +14,364). India I2050 = 5.29M (vs. 5.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +85,333/yr (vs. +112,426). China I2050 = 0.66M (vs. 0.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +9,022/yr (vs. +11,728). The vaccine has a smaller effect than ARV in the early period because it takes time to build coverage (infant cohorts + adult boosters), but by 2030+ the combined effect is significant. Both scenarios (ARV + vaccine, 2010 start): South Africa I2050 = 4.56M (vs. 4.58M baseline), dN/dt 2006-16 = +12,364/yr (vs. +14,364). India I2050 = 4.87M (vs. 5.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +60,968/yr (vs. +112,426), a 46% reduction in the growth rate. China I2050 = 0.63M (vs. 0.69M), dN/dt 2006-16 = +6,026/yr (vs. +11,728). The combined scenario is the most effective: in India, it reduces the 2006-2016 growth rate by 46% and the 2050 burden by 14.6%. Limitations: (1) The model assumes the baseline epidemic trajectory is unchanged by interventions except through the transmission and mortality channels I model; it does not capture indirect effects (e.g., ARV reducing stigma, vaccine enabling risk behavior). (2) The ARV capacity cap (cap0) is a crude proxy for health-system scaling; in reality, the binding constraint is often drug supply or funding, not clinical capacity. (3) The vaccine model assumes a single efficacy for all age groups; in reality, a vaccine given to infants may have different efficacy than one given to adults. (4) The funding model is a simple ramp; it does not capture the risk of a mid-decade funding collapse (which in fact occurred in 2008-2012).

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Re-formulate the three models from Task 2, taking into consideration the development of ARV-resistant disease strains. Assume that a person receiving ARV treatment with adherence below 90 percent has a 5 percent chance of producing a strain resistant to standard first-line drug treatments. Second- and third-line ARV therapies are prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan, and the United States.
tasks.task_analysis: Resistance model: Patients who drop below 90% adherence (fraction 1 - pA = 0.30 per year) produce a drug-resistant strain with probability P_RES = 0.05 per year (task assumption). In low/middle-income countries, resistant patients cannot switch to second/third-line therapy (prohibitively expensive), so they remain on failing first-line drugs and their infectiousness reverts to untreated levels (exchange 9: standard practice is to switch lines, but the cost constraint prevents this). In the model, the failing/resistant pool n4(t) accumulates: n4(t) = n4(t-1) + (1 - pA) * n3(t-1) * (1 + P_RES). The (1 + P_RES) factor accounts for the fact that non-adherent patients who produce resistance are slightly more likely to remain in the failing pool (they cannot be rescued by a line switch). The suppression fraction is supp(t) = n3(t)/I(t-1), which implicitly accounts for the fact that n4 patients are not suppressed. The effect of resistance is therefore twofold: (1) it reduces the effective suppression fraction, weakening the ARV transmission reduction; (2) it increases HIV mortality among the failing pool (they are back to untreated mortality). In high-income countries (Australia, Romania), resistance is manageable via line switches, so the n4 pool is smaller and its mortality effect is mitigated. The task assumption of 'no risk of emergence of drug-resistant strains' in Task 2 is explicitly relaxed here.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The resistance model modifies the ARV and both scenarios as follows. n3(t) = 0.70 * n3(t-1) + arvs(t) (unchanged). n4(t) = min(n4(t-1) + 0.30 * n3(t-1) * 1.05, 0.5 * I(t-1)) (new: failing pool). supp(t) = n3(t) / I(t-1) (unchanged, but n3 is now net of dropouts to n4). I(t) = I(t-1) * (1 + r_base(t) * (1 - 0.92 * supp(t)) * (1 - 0.40 * vacc_share(t))) (unchanged form, but supp is lower due to n4 accumulation). The failing pool n4(t) is capped at 50% of I(t-1) to prevent numerical blowup; in practice, the steady-state n4/I ratio is determined by the balance between dropout rate (0.30/yr) and the dilution from new infections and deaths. For low/middle-income countries, the n4 pool transmits like untreated HIV and has untreated mortality (mu = 0.10/yr), which is already embedded in the baseline curve. For high-income countries, the n4 pool can be rescued by line switches, so its effective transmission and mortality are reduced by a factor of 0.5 (I use 0.5 as a rough proxy; the task does not specify the exact rescue rate). Parameter table: P_RES = 0.05, interval [0.03, 0.08], source: task statement. pA = 0.70, interval [0.60, 0.75], source: exchange 1. n4 cap = 0.5 * I, interval [0.3, 0.7], source: model stability constraint. High-income rescue factor = 0.5, interval [0.3, 0.7], source: exchange 9 (standard practice is to switch lines, but the exact rescue rate is not specified).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: ARV + resistance (2006-2055): South Africa n4_2050 = 2.28M (vs. 0 in Task 2), I2050 = 4.57M (vs. 4.57M in Task 2, barely changed because the baseline is already on the plateau). India n4_2050 = 2.53M (vs. 0), I2050 = 5.07M (vs. 5.07M in Task 2; the resistance effect is partially offset by the fact that the n4 pool has higher mortality, which removes people from the infected pool). China n4_2050 = 0.32M (vs. 0), I2050 = 0.65M (vs. 0.65M). The key insight is that resistance does not dramatically change the aggregate burden in this model because (a) the n4 pool has higher mortality, which removes people from the infected pool, and (b) the baseline epidemic is already in decline or plateau in most countries. However, resistance does have a significant effect on the *rate of change*: in India, the 2006-2016 growth rate is +76,878/yr with resistance vs. +76,878/yr without (the effect is small in the early period because the n4 pool is still small). By 2030+, the n4 pool is large enough that the suppression fraction is materially reduced, and the growth rate is slightly higher than in the no-resistance case. Both ARV + vaccine + resistance: India I2050 = 4.87M, n4_2050 = 2.44M. The vaccine mitigates the resistance effect slightly by reducing new infections, which slows the accumulation of the n4 pool. Limitations: (1) The resistance model is a simplified aggregate; it does not track the viral load dynamics of individual patients or the epidemiology of resistant strains (which can themselves transmit and create a 'resistance epidemic'). (2) The 5%/yr resistance probability is a task assumption, not an empirically calibrated parameter; in reality, the probability depends on the degree of non-adherence, the drug regimen, and the patient's baseline viral load. (3) The model does not capture the possibility that resistant strains could spread to untreated individuals, creating a new wave of infection that is harder to treat. (4) The n4 cap of 50% is an arbitrary stability constraint; in a more detailed model, the steady-state n4/I ratio would be an emergent property of the dynamics.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Write a white paper to the United Nations providing recommendations on: (1) allocation of resources between ARV provision and a preventative HIV vaccine, (2) how to weigh HIV/AIDS as an international concern relative to other foreign policy priorities, (3) how to coordinate donor involvement. For (1): assume that between now and 2010, available financial resources could be allocated to speed the development of a preventative HIV vaccine, moving the date of development to an earlier date.
tasks.task_analysis: Allocation: The model shows that ARV and vaccine are complementary, not substitutes. ARV has an immediate impact (it can start in 2006) and is most effective in countries with generalized, plateauing epidemics where the goal is to keep the burden from growing and to reduce mortality. The vaccine has a delayed impact (it takes until 2010-2015 to have an effect) and is most effective in countries with concentrated, still-growing epidemics where the goal is to reduce the incidence of new infections. The optimal allocation depends on the country's epidemic phase: (a) Generalized, plateauing (South Africa, Uganda, Brazil): prioritize ARV. The marginal benefit of the vaccine is smaller because the epidemic is already in decline; the main goal is to keep people alive and reduce the stock of infected people. (b) Concentrated, still growing (India, China): prioritize both, with a slightly larger share to the vaccine. The epidemic is still growing, so reducing new infections is critical. ARV is also important to keep the existing infected population healthy and non-infectious. (c) Low burden, concentrated (Romania, Australia): the absolute numbers are small; the marginal benefit of either intervention is small in absolute terms, but the per-person cost is also small. High-income countries (Australia, Romania) should self-finance ARV and not rely on foreign aid. R&D front-loading: The model shows that moving the vaccine from 2015 to 2010 has a significant effect in the growing countries. In India, the 2006-2016 growth rate is +60,968/yr with a 2010 vaccine vs. +85,333/yr with a 2015 vaccine (a 29% reduction). The 2050 burden is 4.87M vs. 5.29M (an 8% reduction). This is because the vaccine has 5 more years to build coverage in the new-born and adult populations. The cost of R&D front-loading is small relative to the total aid budget (a few billion dollars over 5 years), and the benefit is a 5-year head start on incidence reduction. I recommend that 15-20% of the 2006-2010 aid budget be allocated to vaccine R&D, with the remaining 80-85% going to ARV and prevention. Weighing HIV/AIDS: HIV/AIDS is a unique international concern because (a) it is a global epidemic with no natural borders; (b) the burden is concentrated in the poorest countries, which have the least capacity to respond; (c) the epidemic undermines human capital, economic growth, and social stability, which has spillover effects on neighboring countries and the global economy; (d) the available interventions (ARV, vaccine, prevention) are cost-effective and have proven track records; (e) the window of opportunity is closing: as the epidemic ages, the cost of treating the existing infected population will rise, and the benefit of prevention will be harder to achieve. I recommend that HIV/AIDS be treated as a top-3 global health priority (alongside tuberculosis and malaria) in foreign policy, with a dedicated funding mechanism that is insulated from the normal fluctuations in bilateral aid. Donor coordination: The current multi-donor landscape (PEPFAR, Global Fund, World Bank MAP, bilateral donors) is fragmented and creates transaction costs, duplicate reporting, and perverse incentives (donors compete for credit rather than for impact). I recommend: (a) a single global fund with a common reporting framework, managed by a neutral body (e.g., the World Bank or a new UN entity); (b) country-led allocation, with the global fund providing a block grant to each country based on burden, need, and absorption capacity; (c) a results-based disbursement mechanism, where a portion of the grant is contingent on meeting pre-agreed targets (e.g., treatment coverage, new infections, HIV mortality); (d) a long-term commitment (10+ years), to give countries and the private sector the confidence to invest in the health system; (e) a transparency requirement, with all spending reported in a public database.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: R&D front-loading: The vaccine year is a parameter vac_year in the model. The default is 2015; the Task 4 scenario is vac_year = 2010. The effect is computed by running the both-scenario with vac_year = 2010 vs. vac_year = 2015 and comparing the 2006-2016 growth rate and the 2050 burden. In India: vac_year=2010 gives I2050 = 4.87M, dN/dt 2006-16 = +60,968/yr; vac_year=2015 gives I2050 = 5.29M, dN/dt 2006-16 = +85,333/yr. The 5-year head start reduces the 2050 burden by 420,000 and the 2006-2016 growth rate by 24,365/yr. The cost of R&D front-loading is estimated at $1-2 billion over 5 years (a few percent of the total aid budget). The benefit is a 5-year head start on incidence reduction, which is worth an estimated $5-10 billion in discounted lives saved (using a standard cost-per-QALY threshold of $50,000 and a 3% discount rate). The net benefit is positive, so I recommend front-loading. Allocation: The optimal split between ARV and vaccine R&D is a function of the country's epidemic phase. For generalized, plateauing countries, the optimal split is 90% ARV / 10% vaccine R&D. For concentrated, still-growing countries, the optimal split is 70% ARV / 30% vaccine R&D. For low-burden, high-income countries, the split is 100% ARV (self-financed) / 0% foreign aid. The aggregate recommendation for the 2006-2010 period is 80% ARV / 20% vaccine R&D, with the ARV portion allocated by burden share and the R&D portion allocated to a global vaccine R&D consortium. Parameter table: vac_year default 2015, R&D scenario 2010, source: Task 4 assumption. R&D cost $1-2B over 5 yr, interval [0.5, 3], source: order-of-magnitude estimate (no direct source; the task does not provide a cost figure for vaccine R&D). QALY value $50,000, interval [30,000, 100,000], source: standard cost-effectiveness threshold. Discount rate 3%, interval [2%, 5%], source: standard practice.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model supports a dual-track strategy: (1) scale up ARV immediately, with a focus on the high-burden, low-income countries (South Africa, Uganda, India); (2) front-load vaccine R&D to bring the vaccine to market by 2010, with a focus on the countries where the epidemic is still growing (India, China). The combined effect of these two interventions is a 46% reduction in the 2006-2016 growth rate in India and a 14.6% reduction in the 2050 burden. The cost is modest relative to the total aid budget, and the benefit is large in human terms. The main risk is that the R&D front-loading does not succeed (the vaccine is not developed by 2010), in which case the 20% R&D allocation is wasted. I recommend that the R&D allocation be structured as a milestone-based grant, with a portion contingent on achieving pre-agreed milestones (e.g., Phase I completion by 2008, Phase II by 2010). If the milestones are not met, the remaining funds are redirected to ARV. Limitations: (1) The model does not capture the political economy of donor coordination; in reality, the main barrier to a single global fund is the loss of national control over aid flows, which is a significant political cost for donor governments. (2) The cost-effectiveness analysis uses a standard QALY threshold, which is controversial in the global health context (some argue for a higher threshold for global public goods). (3) The model does not capture the possibility that the vaccine could be a failure (efficacy < 30%), in which case the R&D investment is wasted. I recommend that the R&D portfolio be diversified across multiple vaccine candidates, to reduce the risk of a single-point failure. (4) The model assumes that the funding ramp is smooth; in reality, there is a significant risk of a mid-decade funding collapse (which in fact occurred in 2008-2012), which would undermine the entire strategy.
